title: A New Feedback Window
subject: rla
passage:
Starting next month, the design office will change how staff comment on draft materials. At present, people can add comments at any point until a project is approved. That flexibility sounds convenient, but teams often receive major suggestions after they have already finished layout, accessibility checks, or printing estimates. A late request to change the audience, reorder an entire brochure, or replace a key image can undo several stages of work at once.

The new process creates a two-day feedback window after each first draft. During that period, reviewers can suggest major changes to content, structure, or direction. After the window closes, comments should focus on errors, safety issues, accessibility problems, or small corrections. A project lead may reopen the broader review if new information appears.

The office is calling the change a guardrail, not a wall. That distinction is deliberate. Managers do not want to silence useful criticism; they want to keep late comments from repeatedly sending projects back to the beginning. The rule is meant to guide timing, while leaving a route for important exceptions.

To make the distinction clearer, the office circulated examples. "Move the emergency number to a more visible place" would remain acceptable at any stage because it concerns safety. "Rewrite the entire introduction in a friendlier voice" would normally belong inside the two-day window. The examples are not meant to settle every disagreement, but managers hope they will reduce arguments about whether a late comment is essential or simply preferable.

Some staff members have welcomed the plan because it makes review responsibilities easier to schedule. Others worry that a short window could reward the fastest reviewers rather than the most thoughtful ones. A designer who is handling several deadlines at once may not have two uninterrupted days to study a draft carefully. In response, the office will test the policy for eight weeks and compare revision time, missed errors, and staff feedback with records from earlier projects.

Managers also plan to track how often project leads reopen the broad review. If exceptions become common, the window may be too rigid or too short. If almost no exceptions occur but staff report that important ideas were withheld, that would be a different warning sign. The trial is supposed to reveal how the rule behaves in practice, not merely whether teams finish faster.

The trial will succeed only if the window creates focus without creating fear. If people rush comments simply to beat the clock, the process may become faster but not better. The office therefore plans to review both speed and quality before deciding whether the policy should continue.
